name: Aleut (Unangax̂)
packetScope: Five substantive works: two renewed APIA sources and three distinct community-government works. No canonical profile or Site files modified. Language-program and NPS wartime review belong to root. Quantity does not establish completeness, community endorsement or initial adequacy.

sources.title: History: Unangax̂, Coastal People of Far Southwestern Alaska
sources.publisher: Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association; Douglas W. Veltre
sources.annotation: APIA publishes this substantial condensation by anthropologist Douglas W. Veltre. Selected sections explain homeland geography, colonial coercion, Pribilof settlement and institutional differences. Undated present-day statistics and broad biological or religious generalizations require separate verification.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read Introduction/Population and Territory, Russian and American Periods, Pribilof Islands, and Unangax̂ Today. This is the web condensation, not inspection of a longer original work.

sources.title: Culture Camp
sources.annotation: A substantive program account describes participation, mentoring and activities offered across different years. Its conflicting 2026/2027 scheduling sentence is excluded. Listed activities do not establish an identical annual curriculum, attendance or measured outcomes.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read the program description and age-group participation sections, web lines 129–205. Embedded videos, mentor biographies and linked media were not reviewed.

sources.title: St. Paul Island Report: 2022 Year End Newsletter
sources.publisher: Aleut Community of St. Paul Island Tribal Government
sources.annotation: The February 2023 issue supplies leadership and conservation-office perspectives on the 2022 crisis and proposed responses. It is one community-government publication, not evidence of universal agreement, realized project outcomes or present fishery conditions.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Population and Territory; Russian and American Periods; Pribilof Islands; Unangax̂ Today
claimBlocks.text: APIA’s historical synthesis places Unangax̂ homelands across the Aleutian chain, Shumagin Islands and western Alaska Peninsula. It describes Russian fur-trade coercion and the compelled movement of Aleutian villagers to the Pribilof Islands, where year-round settlements developed by the early nineteenth century. These colonial movements form part of community history rather than a single unchanging settlement pattern. The account also distinguishes the Aleut Corporation, a shareholder-owned regional business, from APIA, a nonprofit providing tribal services. Neither institution should be substituted for the governments of individual communities.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Program description; children, youth, adults and Elders participation sections
claimBlocks.text: APIA describes its Anchorage culture camp as a gathering connecting participants from the islands, urban Alaska and farther afield. Learning involves different ages: Elders share memories and family connections, children rotate through activities, and older participants choose areas of interest. Activities offered over the years include sewing, basketry and boat-building. The page presents cultural learning as something communities continue to shape in an urban setting. Its historical list of activities should not be read as the schedule for any particular year.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: PDF pages 1–3, 10–11; preamble, Articles V/XI and election certification
claimBlocks.text: The Qawalangin constitution speaks for a particular Unangan government connected with Unalaska, Sedanka and Amaknak islands. Its preamble links self-government with collective cultural, social and economic wellbeing. The posted document provides for a seven-member elected council and protects civil rights, including a qualified right for members to review tribal records. Its certification records an adoption election on May 3, 1997. This is evidence of this government’s constitutional framework at adoption; it does not establish that all Unangax̂ communities share one constitution or that no amendments followed.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Program page and linked public record, PDF pages 1–2
claimBlocks.text: Qawalangin’s environmental program makes another part of self-government visible: maintaining an inventory, reviewing technical documents, seeking community input and coordinating assessment or cleanup. Its linked public record distinguishes proposed investigation from completed actions and identifies work that remains incomplete. These distinctions matter when learning about the continuing responsibilities created by contamination. The record supports an account of oversight and ongoing work; it is not a general assurance that a listed place is safe or unrestricted.

In its February 2023 newsletter, the Aleut Community of St. Paul Island connects economic resilience with the health of the surrounding sea. Leadership describes the crab-fishery crisis and efforts to diversify the island economy. Conservation staff report community engagement around the PRIME initiative and work on Indigenous monitoring, including attention to data sovereignty and intellectual-property rights. These are dated accounts of priorities and work underway, not confirmation that every proposed project was completed. The sanctuary nomination discussed there should not be described as an established marine sanctuary.

identityAndInstitutionNotes: Preserve the canonical name. APIA uses Unangan for an eastern plural, Unangas for an Atka plural and Unangax̂ for a singular in its footer; this does not settle every community’s preferred terminology.
Keep Alutiiq/Sugpiaq access points distinct; do not convert historical external uses of Aleut into an assertion that these peoples are interchangeable.

APIA is a regional nonprofit tribal organization, the Aleut Corporation is a shareholder corporation, and Qawalangin and St. Paul are specific tribal governments. A program publication does not make its publisher the government of all Unangax̂ people.

geographyNotes.note: Selected Population and Territory section supports a scoped Alaska connection, not a cadastral boundary or complete territorial map.
Preamble names Unalaska, Sedanka and Amaknak islands, Alaska; no territorial polygon or current title claim proposed.
St. Paul account supplies a community-specific Pribilof connection; distinguish it from the earlier Aleutian homeland narrative.

coverageGaps: Five selected works do not represent all communities, regional viewpoints or disagreement. Additional island-specific community accounts would improve balance.
Current constitutional amendments, council composition, citizenship rules and legal territorial status were not audited.
The newsletter reports an earlier period; project completion, current fisheries conditions and sanctuary status require separate, current evidence before making present-tense claims.
The contamination record is an administrative collection with inconsistent date residue, not independent confirmation of cleanup effectiveness or safety.
No language-program, full wartime, restricted cultural knowledge or sensitive archaeological-location review was attempted in this packet.
